messages.content: You are a careful experimental physicist.

You are in an unfamiliar physical world. A heavy orange anchor is fixed at x = 0.000, z = 1.500 m; a light blue probe moves around it. Coordinates are sphere centres in metres, x right and z up, y = 0; the grid spacing is 0.10 m. The anchor has mass 1 kg and the probe 0.1 kg. The probe is attracted to the anchor, but the force law of this world may differ from familiar physics and may vary with distance and time.

Your goal is to learn this world well enough to foresee how new scenes will unfold. Later, without any tools, you will see new scenes and choose which image shows the probe's future position.

You may run up to 12 experiments from the menu below, one per turn, with the tool run_experiment. Each experiment places the probe to the right of the anchor at a given distance, launches it with a given velocity at a given world time, and records it at 6 equally spaced moments over the duration. The world returns an image of the panel with the probe drawn at its start and at every recorded moment, fading from faint (start) to solid (end). If the probe reaches the anchor's minimum separation or leaves the field of view, the record stops there. Before each experiment, give in the argument expected_end_m where you expect the probe to be at the end of the record ([x, z] in metres). It is recorded and not scored.

From time to time you will also be shown a new scene in this world and four candidate futures; answer with one letter, then you will see the true outcome.

Let me analyze what I've learned so far from the experiments:

From e49 (1.5m, v=0, t=0.5s, dur=0.4s) and e51 (1.5m, v=0, t=2.5s, dur=0.4s): both show the probe barely moving, with a small trail suggesting slight motion. The probe appears to drift slightly, but the pixel positions are very close to the start, suggesting weak force at this distance (1.5m).

From e25 (1.2m, v=0, t=0.5s, dur=0.4s): similarly small displacement.

From e02 (0.9m, v=0, t=0.5s, dur=0.8s): the probe reached minimum separation quickly - strong attraction at closer distance. This confirms force increases sharply at smaller distances (consistent with inverse power law).

From e50 (1.5m, v=0, t=0.5s, dur=0.8s): probe moved from start toward anchor, ending around 2-3 trail positions, converging distance decreased.

So the pattern: weak attraction at 1.5m, but much stronger close in - consistent with inverse-square or steeper. This is probably just standard gravity-like attraction, pulling the probe toward the anchor, with force increasing as distance decreases.

Now for this checkpoint: probe starts at (1.5, 0.5), anchor at (0.5, 1.2). Separation vector: dx=-1.0, dz=0.7, distance = sqrt(1+0.49)=1.221m. This is moderate distance, similar to the ~1.2m experiments where I saw weak-to-moderate acceleration over 0.4s.

With velocity (0, 0.7) m/s and weak attraction over 0.4s, the probe moves primarily by its initial velocity: dz offset ≈ 0.7*0.4=0.28m, giving z≈0.78. The attraction would pull it toward the anchor (up-left direction, since anchor is up-left of probe), adding a small leftward and upward component beyond pure inertia, and gravity would also curve the path.

Looking at the images: A shows probe moved up and slightly left the most, with highest position. B is somewhat lower, C lower still, D lowest (smallest displacement), with positions trending from upper-left (A) to lower-right (D) in the sequence shown.

Since pure inertial motion predicts z=0.78 (quite high up), and attraction adds extra upward+leftward pull (since anchor is above-left), the actual displacement should be larger than pure inertia alone suggests. That means the probe should move further than simple linear extrapolation - supporting a higher position, i.e., A or B.

Given moderate force at this distance (~1.2m, similar to e25 where displacement was small over 0.4s, just slight motion), the extra pull is modest. Combined with inertial velocity (0.28m upward), I'll estimate final position closer to A.

A
